steps.title: Definition
steps.body: An article is written for publication in a newspaper, magazine, or online platform. It informs, persuades, or entertains a specific audience while following journalistic conventions.

steps.title: Headline Techniques
steps.body: Use alliteration: "Baking Ban Begins" Ask a question: "Is This the End of Free Speech?" Make a bold statement: "Our Schools Are Failing" Use a pun or wordplay: "Storm Brewing Over Tea Tax" Create intrigue: "The Hidden Danger in Your Home"

steps.title: Opening Techniques
steps.body: Start with a dramatic statement Use a rhetorical question Begin with an interesting fact or statistic Open with a brief anecdote or scenario

steps.title: Top Tip
steps.body: Articles are meant to be read quickly. Use short paragraphs, clear topic sentences, and subheadings to guide the reader through your argument.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Write three different headlines for an article about school uniform using different techniques. | What is the "inverted pyramid" structure and when would you use it? | Write an opening paragraph for an opinion article about social media.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Examples: "Uniform Uproar" (alliteration), "Should We Ditch School Uniform?" (question), "The Hidden Cost of School Uniform" (intrigue), "Uniform: Unfair and Unnecessary" (bold statement). | The inverted pyramid puts the most important information first, then supporting details in decreasing order of importance. Used for news articles to ensure key facts aren't cut if space is limited. | Your opening should hook the reader with a dramatic statement, surprising fact, or rhetorical question about social media.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Craft a catchy, relevant headline Hook the reader in your first sentence Use short paragraphs - they're easier to read Include facts, statistics, or quotes for credibility Match your tone to the target publication Use subheadings for longer articles End with a powerful, memorable statement
